questions.q: Architecturally, what does a data catalog actually store and serve?
options: Metadata about data assets, not the underlying data itself
Only business glossary terms
A full copy of every table it indexes
Compiled application code
questions.explain: A catalog is a searchable inventory of metadata — descriptions, owners, tags, lineage — separate from the data it describes.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four core components of a catalog architecture named in this lesson?
options: An API layer
Connectors
A dedicated payment processor
An index/store
questions.explain: The four components are connectors, the index/store, the UI, and the API layer — a payment processor has nothing to do with catalog architecture.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why do most organizations buy a catalog platform rather than build one?
options: Building a catalog is prohibited by most data regulations
Vendors legally require catalogs to be purchased, not built
The connector layer — reliably covering dozens of source-system types — is the genuinely expensive part, not the UI
Catalog UIs are too complex for any internal team to design
questions.explain: The lesson identifies connector maintenance across many source types as the real cost driver behind the build-vs-buy decision.

questions.q: How does a catalog relate to the enterprise metadata architecture covered in Lesson 12?
options: The catalog IS the entire metadata architecture; nothing else consumes it
The catalog replaces the need for a harvesting layer
The catalog is one consumer of the serving layer — alongside things like lineage viewers and access-control engines
The catalog and the metadata architecture are unrelated
questions.explain: Lesson 12 described harvest/store/serve layers; this lesson frames the catalog as one UI/API surface over that same architecture, not a separate architecture of its own.

questions.q: What happens to a catalog's usefulness if its harvesting layer is incomplete, even with a polished UI?
options: It has no effect, because the UI is the only part that matters
The catalog becomes a data dictionary instead
The UI automatically fills in any missing metadata
The catalog remains incomplete — the UI can't fix what the harvesting layer never captured
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that a catalog is only as complete as what its underlying harvesting/storage architecture actually captured.
